_meta.label: Coach notes are written for the debrief. They are not feedback from a real coach.
_meta.keys: notes[momentId][optionId]. Each note names the rubric domain it maps to.

m1.greet: Names plus a specific reference to last session is the level-4 opening (R1, R2). Watch how the discouraged student looks up.
m1.group: A group greeting is fine but sees nobody (rubric Domain 1, level 2). One sentence per student with a real reference changes the room.
m1.cold: A cold open is a named failure mode. The student who already expects to fail reads it as confirmation.

m2.data: Reviewing straight from the tickets is the data loop working (S1, D3). The students whose error you named now have a reason to pay attention.
m2.vague: 'Like last time' targets nothing. The tickets already told you which error to review; using them is the whole point (Domain 5).
m2.skip: Skipping review saves five minutes and costs the session's target. The sign error from the ticket comes straight back.

m3.probe: A question at the spot where the error is, without naming it, lets the student find the fix (Q3, P3). That's the move the whole program is built on.
m3.partial: A partial step jumps straight to ladder rung 3. The student copies it instead of finding it. Try a probing question (rung 0) first.
m3.label: Naming the misconception hands over the diagnosis and lands as a verdict. Name the symptom in a question instead: 'What did the 2 multiply?'
m3.tell: Telling the answer makes the line right and leaves the student's understanding where it was. They produced nothing.

m4.ask-wait: Asking the group and then waiting is where the quiet student gets in. If you spoke again before 3 seconds, the fastest student answered for everyone (Q4).
m4.volunteer: Taking the first hand every time gives the session to one student (R4). The other two learn to wait.
m4.self: Answering your own question turns the group into an audience (rubric Domain 3, level 2).

m5.redirect: Holding the interrupter's idea and handing the turn back is how attention stays distributed (R4).
m5.let: Praising the interrupter in that moment rewards the interruption. The quieter student erased her note; watch for that cue.
m5.move-on: Moving on is neutral for the content and costly for the student who was cut off.

m6.worked: Three failures on the same step is the P7 trigger: acknowledge the frustration, then work a similar problem fully, then return to the original (Q5).
m6.specific: Naming the part that was right is good feedback (F1) and rebuilds some confidence, but after three failures a worked example is the stronger move.
m6.ladder: Another hint after three failures keeps the student in unproductive struggle. P7 says stop climbing.
m6.full: The full solution (rung 5) is a last resort after the worked example. Here it confirms the student 'can't do it' (Q6).
m6.praise: 'You're doing great' after three failures reads as untrue. Specific, process-level feedback works; generic praise doesn't.

m7.why: Confirm briefly, ask one why, and then wait. If you filled the silence yourself, the self-explanation didn't happen (F3, Q4).
m7.similar: Offering a similar problem is a good move (F4, P5). Asking why first would have let her explain the step she got right.
m7.praise: 'Good job' confirms but names nothing she can repeat. Say what in her work was right (F1).

m8.ticket: Protecting the exit ticket and parking the question for next time keeps the data loop intact (S3, D1).
m8.one-more: One more problem is a good instinct at the wrong time. A rushed ticket is weak data for Thursday's review.
m8.skip: Skipping the exit ticket caps Session structure at level 1 on the rubric. Thursday's review has nothing to go on.
